extracted.intended_audience: upper-division undergraduate and beginning graduate students in journalism/mass communication; media scholars and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter framing how to analyze mass media content and the multiple influences that shape it, aimed at students and researchers learning to build theories and conduct content studies (news and entertainment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of media content (quantitative and qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: By content, we mean the complete quantitative and qualitative range of verbal and visual information distributed by the mass media. Quantitative attributes are those that can be measured or counted (e.g., seconds a TV story lasts, column inches); qualitative attributes describe what the coverage was like and are harder to measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative measures to capture amounts and prominence (e.g., placement, seconds, column inches), but assess qualitative attributes (tone, perspective, fairness) for deeper understanding. Qualitative measurement is difficult but often more revealing than counts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare media reality to social reality (social derivation of reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no perfectly objective observer; the best assessment compares media reality with social reality — a socially derived view of what society knows about itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct social reality from diverse sources (personnel files, memos, polls, direct observation) and use it as a benchmark when judging how closely media representations mirror 'reality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis-driven research (the Hypothesis Approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many content studies present expectations and then test one or more hypotheses—relationships between variables that characterize a phenomenon (e.g., event newsworthiness and coverage prominence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define key variables explicitly, operationalize and measure them, state assumptions, and test predicted relationships. Use multiple related hypotheses to build toward theory. Avoid purely descriptive studies without theoretical linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory building: include assumptions, definitions, measures, propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong theories explicitly state assumptions, define key concepts, offer propositions/hypotheses, and suggest ways to measure them (theory may be one hypothesis or many).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing or evaluating work, look for clear assumptions, coherent propositions, and operationalizable measures; recognize that absence of theoretical linkage is a common shortcoming in content studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness → coverage prominence (example hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more newsworthy an event is judged to be, the more prominently it will be covered by the mass media (e.g., front page placement or lead in a newscast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize 'newsworthiness' and 'prominence' (e.g., national vs local significance, placement, length) and test the predicted correlation; use this as a prototypical hypothesis linking content attributes to editorial selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeeping (selection by journalists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists act as gatekeepers who select from among events those that will become 'news' (David Manning White's concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine selection processes and criteria; analyze which events are chosen and which are excluded to understand content formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror approach / null effects (content reflects social reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mirror approach assumes media convey an accurate reflection of social reality. The null effects variant suggests that compromises between information sellers and buyers produce an objective portrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a benchmark hypothesis: test whether content correlates closely with indicators of social reality or results from balancing market forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicator-centered approach (influence of media workers' socialization and attitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is influenced by the psychological attributes of communications personnel—their professional, personal, and political attitudes and training—which shape portrayals (e.g., treating deviant groups as marginal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess journalists' backgrounds, attitudes, socialization, and professional norms to predict content tendencies; consider empirical measures of reporters' demographics, values, and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational routines approach (routines shape content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media content is shaped by the routines and organizational practices of news production (e.g., inverted pyramid, reliance on desk judgments), which structure what is reported and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze newsroom routines, standard operating procedures, story formats, and reliance on other media or official channels; examine how these routines constrain or enable certain kinds of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of influence framework (individual, routines, organization, extramedia, ideology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media content is influenced at multiple levels: individual media workers (backgrounds, attitudes), routines of media work, organizational-level factors (goals, structure, ownership), extramedia forces (sources, advertisers, government, marketplace, technology), and ideological forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media content, identify and separate influences operating at each level and analyze their interconnections (e.g., how individual attitudes interact with routines and organizational constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual media worker influences (backgrounds, roles, ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of individual media workers—gender, ethnicity, education, political and religious attitudes, professional roles and ethics—affect media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and consider how reporters' demographics, career trajectories, and ethical orientations influence story selection, framing, and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational influences (goals, economics, ownership, structure, control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations shape content via goals (primacy of economic goals), economic constraints or dictates, organizational roles and structures, ownership patterns, corporate policies, and mechanisms of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate organizational policies, ownership structures (chains, cross-ownership, multiple media ownership), economic incentives, and internal control systems to explain patterns and slants in content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia influences (sources, advertisers, government, marketplace, technology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forces outside media organizations—official sources, interest groups, public relations, advertisers and audiences, government laws/policies, competition, community relations, institutional affiliations, and technology—affect media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the journalist–source relationship, advertiser pressures, regulatory context, market competition, and technological affordances (e.g., information highways) as explanatory factors for content selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology and paradigms (power, political economy, hegemony, news paradigm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideological forces (e.g., Marxist political economy, cultural studies notions of hegemony, and the news paradigm) influence media content and the maintenance or repair of dominant frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze underlying ideological values, dominant paradigms in news production, and how media reproduce or contest power relations; examine cases of paradigm violation and repair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive vs active conceptualizations of media
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual distinction between viewing media as passive channels that reflect events versus active participants that shape events and meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, decide whether to model media as transmitters of observed reality or as agents that interpret, frame, and even affect events; this choice affects hypotheses and methods.
